opus-5.5.text:
I think it was a very natural, and honestly necessary, transition.

In the early days of Google Brain, and in robotics at Google too, the culture was very bottom-up. A researcher would have an idea, find one or two collaborators, and push it forward. That was wonderful for exploration. A lot of the foundational work came out of that environment, because people had the freedom to try things that looked crazy at the time. In my own area, legged locomotion and sim-to-real, much of our early progress came from small teams that could iterate very quickly without a lot of coordination overhead.

But the nature of the frontier changed. Once it became clear that scale really matters, with more data, bigger models, and more compute, the unit of progress stopped being a single paper from three people. Training a frontier model, or building a robot foundation model that works across many embodiments and tasks, is an engineering and organizational problem as much as a research problem. You need people on data collection, infrastructure, evaluation, hardware, and safety, all moving in the same direction. A loosely organized group just can't marshal those resources efficiently. You end up with ten teams each building their own half-solution.

So bringing Brain and DeepMind together, and organizing around a few big bets, made a lot of sense to me. Competitively, too, the industry was moving very fast, and focus became a survival skill.

That said, I don't think it's free. There's a real tension. When everything is organized around large coordinated efforts, you risk losing the long-tail exploration, the weird ideas that don't fit the current roadmap but turn out to matter five years later. Many of today's breakthroughs started as side projects nobody was asking for. So the challenge for leadership, and for researchers like me, is to keep some space for that curiosity-driven work while still contributing to the big shared goals.

In robotics specifically, I feel we're right at that inflection point. For a long time it was a field of many small, specialized solutions: one controller for walking, another for grasping. Now we're starting to see that robotics may follow the same path as language, toward general models trained at scale. That pushes us toward bigger, more coordinated teams. But robotics also still has a lot of unsolved fundamental problems, like physical data scarcity, safety, and the embodiment gap, where a small group with a fresh idea can still change the direction of the field.

So my view is that the shift was right for this moment, but the best organizations will be the ones that can do both: concentrate force on the big bets and protect the small, curious explorations at the edges.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I first joined Google, the culture was very bottom-up. You'd have a small group, maybe three to five people, and you'd pick a problem you cared about, write a paper, and move on. That was the Google Brain style, and it was incredibly fun for a researcher. A lot of my early work on robot learning came out of exactly that kind of freedom.

But I think the shift was inevitable once we saw what scaling could do. When the models started getting really large, it became clear that no small team could train or even properly evaluate them alone. You need people on data, people on infrastructure, people on evaluation, people on safety. Gemini is a good example. It's not one lab's project, it's hundreds of people coordinated toward a single goal. And when the DeepMind and Brain merger happened, part of the motivation was exactly that: concentrate the talent and compute instead of having many parallel efforts that each only get a slice.

There's a real tradeoff, though. The loosely organized model generates a lot of diversity. Some ideas that looked strange at the time, like the Transformer, came out of a few people just exploring. In a big coordinated effort, you optimize for the thing you already decided to build, and it's harder to protect those side explorations. I think the leadership is aware of this, and you still see some room for exploratory work, but the balance has definitely moved.

For my own area, robotics, I actually think the larger team structure has helped. Robotics is a systems problem. You need hardware, data collection, simulation, learning, all working together, and that's hard to do with three people. Work like RT-2 or the Gemini Robotics efforts only happened because the organization was willing to put many people behind one direction. So personally I've been quite happy with it, even if I miss some of the old spontaneity.

astra-6.text:
I think it reflects a change in what it takes to do impactful research. In robotics, for example, a good learning algorithm is only one part of the picture. You also need hardware, data collection, simulation, and reliable infrastructure. Coordinating those pieces takes a team with a shared direction.

The benefit is that you can tackle problems that would be very difficult for a few researchers working independently. The risk is that coordination becomes too rigid, and people have less room to pursue an unexpected idea. Research needs that freedom because you don’t always know in advance which approach will work.

So I don’t see it as choosing between individual creativity and large teams. The challenge is to give people a common goal and strong shared infrastructure while leaving enough autonomy to explore. If you can preserve that balance, the scale can be a real advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tradeoff. In a loosely organized research environment, people have more freedom to explore ideas that may not fit an immediate product goal. That freedom can lead to unexpected discoveries. But when you want to turn a research result into something reliable and useful at scale, you need coordination across many different areas.

The risk is that coordination becomes bureaucracy, and researchers spend more time aligning than experimenting. So I wouldn’t frame it as one model replacing the other completely. The challenge is to give large teams a clear shared objective while preserving room for individuals and small groups to try things that might fail. You want the benefits of scale without losing that exploratory spirit.
